title: Adaptive maintenance cadence and capacity-safeguard reservations for sustained throughput
creator: Priya Rao
description:
Problem: Scheduled and unscheduled maintenance on Dedicated fleets currently causes transient throughput regressions and customer visible latency spikes. Existing drain logic is conservative (drain-first, then prewarm on replacement) and doesn't coordinate with autoscaler reservations or per-customer throughput commitments. This results in either over-provisioning (higher cost) or SLO violations during maintenance windows.

Goal: Build an Adaptive Maintenance Cadence (AMC) system that coordinates maintenance actions with a capacity-safeguard reservation layer so drains/upgrades happen without violating per-customer throughput contracts. AMC should: 1) pre-reserve ephemeral throughput lanes before host drains, 2) issue tokenized eviction quotas per-maintenance-event that limit parallel evictions, 3) integrate with the autoscaler to spin up warm hosts and prewarm KV caches ahead of traffic shift, and 4) provide observability and rollback triggers tied to SLO/latency gates.

Scope: This ticket covers design and implementation of the orchestration layer (maintenance cadence engine), the eviction-quota token service, autoscaler integration hooks, and operational dashboards/runbooks. It excludes tenant billing changes and dedicated UI polish (those will be follow-ups).

High-level design: 1) Maintenance cadence engine (MCE) evaluates window, SLOs, and available spare capacity -> emits a plan of staged evictions. 2) For each stage, MCE requests N tokens from the Eviction Quota Service (EQS). Tokens represent capacity rights to evict hosts without affecting throughput contracts. 3) EQS consults the Capacity Safeguard Registry (CSR) which tracks live reservations and per-tenant throughput guarantees, and either approves token allocations or returns a reduced allocation with suggested backoff. 4) When tokens granted, autoscaler is signalled to provision replacement hosts in parallel with KV cache prewarm jobs. 5) Drainer executes staged drains with soft-eviction semantics (grace period + traffic shed thresholds) and releases tokens on completion. 6) Observability layer measures throughput delta vs contract and triggers halting/rollback if thresholds exceeded.

Non-goals: full UI for booking slots, tenant-facing reservation APIs (future), rewriting existing autoscaler algorithms (only integration hooks).

Engineering trade-offs considered: - Tokenized approach keeps decisioning centralized and auditable but adds a control-plane dependency (EQS). We mitigate with EQS replication and local read-caches. - Conservative traffic-shed thresholds reduce risk of SLO violations but slow maintenance cadence; we implement adaptive thresholds based on current load percentiles. - Prewarming increases short-term cost; we'll gate warm-up by expected SLA impact to minimize waste.
acceptance_criteria: MCE can schedule a staged maintenance plan that limits parallel host evictions to an EQS-granted token count
EQS enforces token allocations and persists ephemeral reservations across controller restarts
Autoscaler accepts prewarm hooks and can provision replacement hosts within configured lead time in 90% of test runs
KV cache prewarm workflow can populate prefix/KV for replaced hosts before traffic cutover in canary tests
Observed p95 latency for served requests remains within +10% of baseline during a simulated maintenance window for target tenants
Telemetry surfaces token allocation, stage progress, throughput delta, and an automatic rollback trigger when customer_impact > medium
